options: A. Alphabetically by the publisher's city of origin, followed by the book's page count.
B. Chronologically by the year the book was acquired by the local library branch.
C. Numerically by subject into ten main classes (000 to 999) with decimal subdivisions.
D. By cover size and binding color so reference encyclopedias are shelved next to paperback fiction.

B. Chronologically by the year the book was acquired by the local library branch.
C. Numerically by subject into ten main classes (000 to 999) with decimal subdivisions.

misconception_pool.misconception: Beginners often believe librarians memorize the location of every physical book in the building.
misconception_pool.fact: Librarians rely on systematic alphanumeric classification schemes like Dewey Decimal or Library of Congress call numbers.

misconception_pool.misconception: Dewey Decimal call numbers are shelved by whole-number value after the decimal point, placing 598.12 after 598.2.
misconception_pool.fact: Dewey Decimal numbers are read digit by digit after the decimal point, so 598.12 is shelved before 598.2 on the shelf.

misconception_pool.misconception: Keyword searches and subject heading searches in a computerized library catalog return the exact same list of books.
misconception_pool.fact: Subject searches match standardized controlled vocabulary tags, whereas keyword searches scan titles and notes for any matching word.

misconception_pool.misconception: Fiction novels in a public library are arranged numerically by Dewey Decimal class numbers just like nonfiction books.
misconception_pool.fact: Most public libraries shelve general fiction alphabetically by the author's last name rather than by numeric subject codes.

misconception_pool.misconception: Reference section encyclopedias and atlases can be checked out for home reading using a standard library card.
misconception_pool.fact: Non-circulating reference materials must remain inside the library building so all patrons have immediate access to them.

misconception_pool.misconception: Beginners assume careers requiring heavy reading are confined to traditional author or librarian roles.
misconception_pool.fact: Reading intensive careers span diverse industries including intellectual property law, clinical informatics, and policy research.

misconception_pool.misconception: Every staff member working behind a public library desk holds the same job title and Master of Library Science degree.
misconception_pool.fact: Libraries employ pages, technicians, and ALA-accredited master's-level librarians who have distinct credentials and pay scales.

misconception_pool.misconception: Careers centered on reading skills are limited to classroom English teachers, book editors, and public librarians.
misconception_pool.fact: Technical writers, paralegals, intelligence analysts, medical coders, and archivists all rely heavily on advanced reading skills.

misconception_pool.misconception: University tuition is the only out-of-pocket expense required to enter a certified reading or library profession.
misconception_pool.fact: Entering the field often includes licensing exam fees, unpaid practicum hours, background checks, and continuing education costs.

misconception_pool.misconception: Digital publishing and artificial intelligence tools have eliminated the need for human editors and technical proofreaders.
misconception_pool.fact: Organizations still require skilled human editors and information specialists to verify accuracy, legal compliance, and clarity.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When using a library catalog to locate nonfiction research materials, how does the Dewey Decimal Classification system organize books on the shelves?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When using a library catalog to locate nonfiction research materials, how does the Dewey Decimal Classification system organize books on the shelves?
options: A. Alphabetically by the publisher's city of origin, followed by the book's page count.
B. Chronologically by the year the book was acquired by the local library branch.
C. Numerically by subject into ten main classes (000 to 999) with decimal subdivisions.
D. By cover size and binding color so reference encyclopedias are shelved next to paperback fiction.
choices: A. Alphabetically by the publisher's city of origin, followed by the book's page count.
B. Chronologically by the year the book was acquired by the local library branch.
C. Numerically by subject into ten main classes (000 to 999) with decimal subdivisions.
D. By cover size and binding color so reference encyclopedias are shelved next to paperback fiction.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Numerically by subject into ten main classes (000 to 999) with decimal subdivisions, followed by the author's cutter code so books on the same topic sit together.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The Dewey Decimal system groups nonfiction books by subject using three-digit numbers (000-999) and decimal extensions, making it easy to browse related works on the same topic.
